stories.title: Terror from the skies: drones are redefining warfare in Sudan, and massacring its civilians
stories.summary: View image in fullscreen Terror from the skies: drones are redefining warfare in Sudan, and massacring its civilians Composite: Guardian Design / Getty Images Strikes with huge death tolls are an increasing occurrence as UAVs ‘bring the war to places that were once safe’ The first drone struck the busy transport hub near a market in Al-Dibab as hundreds of people gathered to board trucks to take them back to their homes. Ten minutes later on the evening of 18 October, a second drone hit the same site in the town in West Kordofan state, Sudan . At least 139 people were killed. Eight days after the “double-tap” attack – designed to maximise casualties by killing and injuring emergency responders, volunteers and bystanders on top of the original victims – a drone hit a busy market in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur. Emergency Lawyers, a rights group tracking violence in Sudan, put the death toll from that attack at 103. “I lost my 19-year-old son,” a Nyala resident told Agence France-Presse. “We buried him alongside more than 70 bodies in a single site.” View image in fullscreen The remains of Alneam market after a drone strike in the disputed Abyei region along the border between South Sudan and Sudan last month.

stories.title: Arrested generals and a threatened VP: President's son fuels Ugandan succession fever
stories.summary: Image source, Uganda People's Defence Force (UPDF) Image caption, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba has signalled his intention to run for president in the next elections By Wycliffe Muia Published 14 November 2026, 00:03 GMT In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief. Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks. stories.title: Neither war nor peace in Tigray - is Ethiopia's latest conflict really over?
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Pro-government forces marched into Tigray's capital less than two weeks after the war began By Michael Teferi ,Â BBC Africa Â and Â Yemane Nagish ,Â BBC Tigrinya Published 13 November 2026 Running a hair salon in Mekelle, capital of Ethiopia's troubled northern Tigray region, is not easy at the moment. "People can't prioritise beauty over daily basic needs. For many residents, thinking about self-care is a luxury, at a time when they can't feed their kids," Firut Me'ar, who runs a salon in the city, tells the BBC. After a brief war, the city is under the control of the national army but life is far from normal, says Firut, a single mother of a 10-year-old daughter. "Things are better than during the war, but people still have no money, no morale. Business is almost non-existent," she says, her voice shaking with emotion. Above all, she says people are worried about what the future holds. "There is uncertainty about what comes next." Fighting broke out in late September between the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF), the party that had run Tigray for decades, and the national army - a resumption of the two-year civil war that officially ended in 2022.

stories.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
stories.summary: ‘I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey’ … Simbarashe Kundizeza View image in fullscreen ‘I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey’ … Simbarashe Kundizeza Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-written’ The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation. Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter , which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October. Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated. The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement : “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.” She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation. “Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.” Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.

The event will introduce RESILAFRICA - the proposed Africa Food Systems Resilience Flagship - an initiative that aims to connect existing programmes, financing instruments and technical expertise to help African countries anticipate climate-related and other shocks, protect agricultural production and livelihoods, and invest in long-term resilience. The proposed framework supports the Bank Group's Four Cardinal Points strategic vision, particularly the priority to build resilient infrastructure and competitive value chains. By connecting climate-risk intelligence, resilient agricultural infrastructure, markets and investment, it could help protect productive assets, strengthen regional value chains and support Africa's agricultural transformation. Why it matters Droughts, floods, extreme heat and disruptions to agricultural input and food markets threaten food security, livelihoods and economic development across Africa.

And the Kenyan cabinet secretary for health, Aden Duale, said at a news conference that the last 11 people being monitored for Ebola symptoms had also been discharged after completing a 21-day quarantine period. “For the first time since this outbreak began, Kenya has no patient under treatment and no contact in quarantine,” he said. The milestone is further evidence that countries have succeeded in containing the small number of cases, most coming in from the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the outbreak continues to spread. stories.title: Des harkis réclament justice pour le traitement de leurs morts dans des camps en France dans les années 1960 : « Nous avons été traités avec mépris par la République »
stories.summary: Cinq familles de harkis, dont des membres ont vécu dans le camp de Saint-Maurice-l’Ardoise (Gard), après leur arrivée d’Algérie en 1962, veulent comprendre pourquoi leurs proches ont été enterrés en catimini et pourquoi les ossements de certains d’entre eux ont disparu. Elles ont déposé plainte le 9 novembre.

stories.title: Le romancier Kamel Daoud condamné à cinq ans de prison en Algérie pour son roman « Houris »
stories.summary: Son ouvrage, récompensé du prix Goncourt en 2024, explore la « décennie noire » algérienne, qui a fait 200 000 morts entre 1992 et 2002. Cette condamnation concerne une affaire l’opposant à Saâda Arbane, une Algérienne qui avait accusé l’auteur d’avoir volé son histoire tragique.

stories.title: Controversial kinship: From colonial rule to the Holocaust?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5PGDc Prefer DW on Google European colonialism was marked by the — often extremely violent — exploitation of people and resources. [Pictured: Clearing of land by setting grass on fire during a German research expedition to Tendaguru in German East Africa, 1909–1913] Image: Archiv/Museum für Naturkunde Advertisement Racial hierarchy, dehumanization, concentration camps, settler expansion in the name of "living space," collective punishment and mass violence: At first glance, the continuities between colonial and Nazi violence appear obvious. In 1941, Nazi dictator Adolf Hitler himself compared Eastern Europe to "Germany's India" after the British colonial model, declaring that "like the English, we shall rule this empire with a handful of men." But the extent to which Nazism was shaped by the age of empire, and whether the two systems of violence can even be compared, remains the subject of intense debate. This is particularly true in Germany, where the fear is often expressed that any comparison risks relativizing or minimizing Nazi crimes, and particularly the Holocaust . Others have argued that the intense focus on the Nazi era has, at least in part, come at the expense of a meaningful reckoning with Germany's colonial history. 'Murder for the very purpose of murder': The industrialized mass murder carried out in Nazi death camps such as Belzec, Sobibor, Treblinka and Auschwitz-Birkenau had no direct precedent in colonial history. [Pictured: Cans of Zyklon B gas, Auschwitz-Birkenau, German Nazi concentration and extermination camp in Poland] Image: Taiftin/Depositphotos/IMAGO "I do think this is nonsense," says Stephan Malinowski, a Professor of Modern European History at the University of Edinburgh. "If it were true, then all other colonial countries who are not discussing the Holocaust, like Great Britain for example, or France or Spain or Portugal, they would then supposedly be very, very attentive to colonial crimes and to colonial history, which it seems to me is not the case." "Controversial Kinship: Colonial and National Socialist Violence," a new exhibition at the German Historical Museum in Berlin curated by Malinowski, does not aim to settle the debate but to tell its story. From colonial brutality to Nazi rule The exhibition begins with a hippopotamus-hide whip used in African colonies displayed alongside a canister of Zyklon B, the poison used in Nazi gas chambers.

stories.title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
stories.summary: Lewis Hamilton with members of the Egyptian Red Crescent near the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and the Gaza Strip Photograph: Reuters View image in fullscreen Lewis Hamilton with members of the Egyptian Red Crescent near the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and the Gaza Strip Photograph: Reuters Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory. The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire. “I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine . I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October. A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

stories.title: Kenyan Domestic Worker Sentenced to 100 Lashes in Saudi Arabia
stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT A Saudi court has sentenced a domestic worker from Kenya to 100 lashes for giving birth outside marriage. The ruling, issued last month, shows the limits of a decade of social and legal reforms in a kingdom where women can be jailed and punished for “illegal pregnancy.” The sentence is a harsh turn in what has been a terrifying ordeal for a mother who has tried for more than a year to return to Kenya with her child but has been blocked at every turn. The mother, Esther Wanja Muthoni, is one of thousands of East African domestic workers who were recruited to work as housekeepers and nannies in Saudi Arabia. A New York Times investigation last year showed how Ms. Muthoni and others wind up trapped in a bureaucratic maze if they become pregnant.

stories.title: Immigrants Are Being Systematically Returned Home Despite Court Orders
stories.summary: Mustapha Camara worked 12-hour shifts during the pandemic as a nurse in Nebraska. In July, ICE agents arrested him in front of his family home. A judge had already prohibited the U.S. government from deporting him to Gambia, where he risked persecution. Here’s how he ended up there anyway. Mustapha Camara and immigrants like him had court protections that they thought made them safe from the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign.

stories.title: U.S. Global Health Strategy Jeopardizes Prevention of Pandemics, Experts Warn
stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Country by country, the Trump administration has been negotiating secretive agreements with nations across Africa to provide health aid under strict conditions. The agreements, structured to benefit the United States, are undermining efforts to prepare the world for the next pandemic, putting even Americans at risk, public health experts warn. In one striking example, under an agreement signed in February that was never made public, the United States is set to stop funding health care workers in the Democratic Republic of Congo by the end of the year. Congo has been struggling to contain an Ebola outbreak that has topped 10,000 cases and has spread to two other regions of Africa. The plan, a copy of which was obtained by The New York Times, provides Congo with $900 million over the next five years, and was signed before the Ebola outbreak was detected.

stories.title: Abandoned and traumatised: child refugees at ‘violent’ breaking point in Egypt after fleeing Sudan war
stories.summary: Traumatised by war and stuck in poverty, most of the 400,000 or so Sudanese child refugees now living in Egypt are a generation in limbo, support workers say. Illustration: Patrycja Podkościelny/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Traumatised by war and stuck in poverty, most of the 400,000 or so Sudanese child refugees now living in Egypt are a generation in limbo, support workers say. Illustration: Patrycja Podkościelny/The Guardian Abandoned and traumatised: child refugees at ‘violent’ breaking point in Egypt after fleeing Sudan war Three years of conflict has left hundreds of thousands of Sudanese children out of school and vulnerable to gangs and drugs M ounds of rubbish, the stench of raw sewage and, at night, roaming drug dealers and gangs. These are the streets of a forsaken neighbourhood in Cairo that Sudanese children call home, after fleeing the violence of their country’s civil war . It is here that Tala*, a social worker, spends her days trying to bring deeply traumatised war refugees back from the brink.

stories.title: The legacy of South Africa’s first Black showjumper and his horse-riding school in Soweto
stories.summary: View image in fullscreen The legacy of South Africa’s first Black showjumper and his horse-riding school in Soweto A local BMX rider shows off his skills to Enos Mafokate on an afternoon ride through the streets of Soweto. Photograph: Karabo Mooki Enos Mafokate began his career as a stable hand and went on to become a world-class athlete during the apartheid era. In September 2026, aged 80, Enos died in Johannesburg – but his legacy endures through his horse-riding school and the generations of pupils he inspired In a historically wealthy sport dominated by the white elite and plagued by its colonial reign, a Black athlete draped in a red coat represented his nation. This is the remarkable story of Enos Mafokate and the legacy he worked so hard to create. A professional equestrian rider, Enos began his career as a stable hand and went on to become a world-class athlete during the apartheid era in South Africa .

stories.title: From the streets of Lagos to the Chanel catwalk: how a creative’s thrift-shop style took her to Paris
stories.summary: Rachel Ojuromi models clothes sourced from markets and secondhand shops in her Lagos videos. Photograph: SR Odey/Handout View image in fullscreen Rachel Ojuromi models clothes sourced from markets and secondhand shops in her Lagos videos. Photograph: SR Odey/Handout From the streets of Lagos to the Chanel catwalk: how a creative’s thrift-shop style took her to Paris Rachel Ojuromi and her stylist friend Debby Fasingha recreated high-end designs in effortlessly cool videos shot around the city. Then the fashion house came calling B efore Paris, there was Lagos, with its busy markets, roadside stalls and maze of disorderly streets. And then there was Rachel Ojuromi, sashaying through it all and turning the everyday into an unlikely catwalk.

stories.title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven
stories.summary: People at the scene of the collision in Giza province. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People at the scene of the collision in Giza province. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least seven President orders prompt investigation after one train derails in collision in al-Ayyat about 50km from Cairo Seven people were killed and at least 125 injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of the Egyptian capital, Cairo, officials said. The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 50km (30 miles) south of Cairo, when a train travelling to Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry. An inspection indicated that the Cairo-Aswan train had been stationary on the same track, officials said.

stories.title: After suffering its worst election result, what's next for the ANC — and for South Africa?
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5PNPy Prefer DW on Google A new era: Coalition governments are no longer the exception in South African politics Image: Themba Hadebe/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement South Africa's governing African National Congress (ANC) party is forced to confront its worst electoral setback to date after securing under 31% of the vote in the country's significant local government elections; party leaders themselves have described the result as "catastrophic." This outcome marks a steep decline for the party that had once led South Africa's liberation struggle; the party that had dominated the country's political landscape since the end of apartheid in 1994. The result reflects growing public frustration about the ANC's lack of performance in key areas such as skyrocketing unemployment, poor service delivery, local governance failures and years of graft and corruption — sometimes at the highest levels of government. So what comes next for the ANC — and for South Africa ? After years of dominating the political scene, the ANC's future now looks increasingly unstable Image: Leandre Steenberg/Matrix Images/picture alliance Voters express growing frustration and despair Tasnim Essop, a researcher at the Society, Work and Politics Institute (SWOP) at the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, says it is time for the party to undertake some serious introspection. She believes that the ANC has to confront a long list of difficult questions about governance, leadership and accountability. "You're talking about issues like water, electricity, housing, public services at the basic municipal level.

stories.title: Footage shows derailed carriages after fatal train crash in Egypt
stories.summary: Footage shows derailed carriages after fatal train crash in Egypt Footage shows derailed carriages after fatal train crash in Egypt Close A train collision has killed at least seven people and injured dozens in northern Egypt. Footage showed multiple overturned carriages and dozens of people surrounding them. One train was travelling from Giza to the Fayoum oasis, south west of Cairo, while the other was heading from Cairo to Aswan in the south. It is yet unclear what caused the accident but Egyptian President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi said an investigation was underway and would "hold accountable anyone who proves their negligence". Read more about the train collision in Egypt.

stories.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
stories.summary: Daniel Oyegade on the shoot for Homage, a See My World production. Photograph: Omar Balaa View image in fullscreen Daniel Oyegade on the shoot for Homage, a See My World production. Photograph: Omar Balaa How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester See My World, an event highlighting the pan-African thought via film, poetry and dance, builds on momentum sparked by local activists and creatives African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester . See My World , a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November. The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

stories.title: South Africa’s Politics May Never Be the Same Again
stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Few things unite South Africans like a dry faucet. That’s what thousands of residents of Africa’s richest city, Johannesburg, woke up to on Wednesday before voting in local government elections. From the impoverished mostly Black township of Diepsloot to the racially mixed upper-middle-class Midrand to exclusive Hyde Park, which the president calls home, many voters expressed the same frustration as they left the polls. “Now, we don’t have water,” said Luleka Ngqangqashe, 35 and unemployed. “Imagine.” Some chalked up the Election Day outages to divine timing, others to political sabotage and still others to, well, life in Johannesburg. In any case, they were a reminder of the government failures that led the overwhelming majority of voters in this city of nearly five million people to vote against the nation’s once-dominant political, social and moral force: the African National Congress. With most of the votes tallied by Sunday, the A.N.C. was projected to win around 20 percent of the vote in Johannesburg, down from 33 percent in the last local election five years ago.

stories.title: Islamist Militant Attack Forces Patients to Flee Ebola Clinic in Congo
stories.summary: Advertisement SKIP ADVERTISEMENT Militants affiliated with the Islamic State burned down a health center treating Ebola patients in the Democratic Republic of Congo this week, forcing infected patients to flee amid violence that killed dozens of people, according to health and United Nations officials. At least 48 people were killed in the attacks, officials said. It started late Thursday with a series of attacks in and around Cantine-Aloya, a village about 28 miles west of Beni, a city in eastern Congo. Several dozen homes and shops were burned, forcing residents to flee the area. Two other health facilities were also set on fire.
